The Consumer Rights Act 2015

Changes to Consumer Protection Laws, Coming into effect Today, The 1st of October 2015

What has Happened?

The UK government has streamlined 7 different laws into a single new Consumer Rights Act 2015 and has strengthened consumer protection for all purchases in several key areas, including Digitally Distributed goods such as games which were previously not explicitly regulated by law.

What the Consumer Rights Act Says

Goods must be of acceptable quality, based on what a reasonable person would expect, accounting for price

The product must work and be of appropriate quality:

I’m looking at you buggy AAA titles and dysfunctional Indie releases!

Goods must be fit for purpose. If the consumer has a particular purpose in mind, which must be made clear

The product must perform as would be reasonably expected to the stated purpose:

I’m looking at you ‘interactive novels’ masquerading as games!

Goods must meet the expectations of the consumer

The information which has been provided to the customer must be honest:

I’m looking at you journalists who are misselling games due to friendships and cartels with developers and publishers! Now the price of that will fall directly on those developers and publishers.

Important Changes to the Law

This is the first time that rights of the consumer for digital distribution have been formally made into a concrete and clear set of laws and expectations.

This includes that consumers of digitally distributed goods can expect goods which work properly, which are distributed under fair contract, where the business must act competitively.

There is now greater flexibility for public enforcers such as Trading Standards to act on the behalf of consumers and there will be Alternative Dispute Resolution should the company and the customer be unable to agree on recompense for misselling.

Individual Consumers or Consortiums now have the right to sue Companies on the behalf of larger groups.

That means that active groups such as PCMasterRace , KotakuInAction , #GamerGate and others will be able to spontaneously organise take companies to court if you break the above laws on behalf of all UK gamers.
